gap: No result ChatGPT got works out the cost per watt-hour of the AC power banks it recommended: on maker stores today the airline-legal Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC costs $2.63 per Wh ($249.95 / 95 Wh), while the 128 Wh BLUETTI Elite 10 Mini costs $0.93 per Wh ($119 / 128 Wh). That is 2.8x more per Wh to stay under 100 Wh.
standout_why: I compared against thunderboltlaptop.com (Wh, AC watts and weights for no-name 27,000 mAh banks; no prices, no $/Wh, no runtimes), geekchamp.com (works out $/Wh and runtime at 80% only for 230-288 Wh stations and a $76 Daran; for the Sherpa 100AC it gives no AC wattage, weight or price), and engadget.com (Sherpa $250, a 6%-to-72% MacBook Pro result and about 60% average efficiency, but no per-Wh cost and no comparison with a mini station). None of them puts the flight-legal AC banks next to the cheapest mini station on cost per Wh.
decides: It doesn't change the pick, it states what the pick costs. If the shopper flies, the Sherpa 100AC (95 Wh) still wins, and the page should say they pay about $2.63/Wh for the airline-legal size against $0.93/Wh for the Elite 10 Mini. If the bank never goes on a plane, the Elite 10 Mini gives 35% more Wh, twice the AC wattage (200 W vs 100 W) and LiFePO4 cells for less than half the price. That makes it the value pick for car, desk or outage use. Omni 20+ ($249) sits at the Sherpa's price point, so it competes on weight, not on $/Wh.

findings.label: Engadget's average delivered efficiency across tested laptop banks
findings.source_title: The best laptop power banks for 2026 | Engadget
findings.note: Quote: 'I averaged about a 60-percent efficiency rate.' Engadget also says 'Plugging a power adapter into the AC port only wastes energy through conversion' and keeps the AC port for devices that can't use USB. Applied as a planning figure at a 60 W AC load: Sherpa 95 x 0.60 / 60 = 0.95 h; Elite 10 Mini 128 x 0.60 / 60 = 1.28 h. These are estimates, not measurements, and the 60% is Engadget's USB-path average, not an AC measurement.
